assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, built on Katori's magic-wavelength proposal, combine thousands of atoms with optical-frequency coherence to reach fractional uncertainties near 1e-18. This is a new way of measuring time, and it enables tests of fundamental constants, relativistic geodesy and a path toward redefining the second. It fits my view that progress is limited by how precisely we can measure.
assessment.attribution: Katori made the original magic-wavelength lattice proposal and the first demonstrations with strontium. Ye's JILA group brought the clocks to the lowest systematic uncertainty and ran the key comparisons. The two names form a clean, natural pair. Others, such as Lemke and Ludlow, are not in the credited list.
assessment.maturity: Mature in the lab, with independent confirmation across several groups and institutes (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE). The redefinition of the second is still pending, but the physics is stable and recognition is timely.
uncertainties: Overlap with Ye's role in frequency combs, already recognised in 2005 (Hall and Hänsch), and with ion clocks recognised in 2012 (Wineland); the committee may see the clock as an extension.
I recall but have not verified the latest uncertainty figures and the status of the redefinition discussions.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Matter-wave interferometry with atoms gives inertial sensing, gravimetry, tests of the equivalence principle and measurements of G and the fine-structure constant. It is a precision-measurement method that has opened new experiments and is now moving into field instruments such as gravity gradiometers and navigation.
assessment.attribution: Pritchard demonstrated the first atom interferometers and atom optics. Bordé provided the theoretical framework and the Ramsey-Bordé interferometer. Kasevich and Chu made the leap to high-precision light-pulse interferometers. Chu is not on the credited list, which makes the configuration awkward, but the three named people are defensible.
assessment.maturity: The field has been mature for decades. Demonstrations are confirmed by many independent groups. Large-scale and space-based versions are still developing.
uncertainties: Credit for the light-pulse method overlaps with Chu (Nobel 2018 for cooling) and Chu's group is not in the list.
Priority between Bordé and Pritchard for the foundational ideas is partly a matter of how one defines an atom interferometer.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical readout and coherent control of single NV and related defect spins in solids has led to nanoscale magnetometry, thermometry and sensing in biological samples and condensed matter, and to room-temperature solid-state qubits. It is a measurement technique that opened new observation capabilities across physics, chemistry and biology.
assessment.attribution: Wrachtrup and colleagues (with Jelezko) demonstrated optical detection of single NV spins in 1997. Awschalom led semiconductor and defect spin coherence, and Lukin led sensing and many-body protocols. Walsworth is also credited, so the choice of three is contestable. Gruber, Jelezko, Taylor and others are not in the list.
assessment.maturity: Experiments are widely reproduced and applications are growing, though many are still demonstrations. Recognition is plausible now and the field is far from saturated.
uncertainties: Attribution is diffuse: the single-defect detection, the sensing protocols and the quantum-register work are different contributions.
Practical advantage over existing sensors in real applications is not yet fully settled.
Lukin appears in other candidates, so a split of recognition across lists is possible.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices realised the Hubbard model in controllable form: the superfluid to Mott insulator transition, fermionic Hubbard physics and single-site quantum gas microscopy. This is a clear experimental platform for quantum simulation, with direct observation of many-body states.
assessment.attribution: Greiner and Bloch (with Hänsch) did the Mott insulator experiment. Esslinger led fermionic lattices and Hubbard studies. Bloch and Greiner also developed quantum gas microscopes. Jaksch, Zoller and Cirac made the key theoretical proposals; the three experimentalists listed give a coherent prize but leave the proposers out, which creates an attribution tension.
assessment.maturity: Replicated by many groups, widely used, and recognition follows the 2001 BEC prize. The quantum-advantage claim for simulation is still developing.
uncertainties: Theory proposals by Zoller, Cirac and Jaksch preceded the experiments, so an experiment-only prize may be seen as incomplete.
Overlap with candidates B020 and B031 under the same quantum-simulation theme.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Topological insulators are a conceptually important class of materials with robust edge or surface states and large follow-on activity. The quantum spin Hall prediction and its HgTe confirmation are clean cases of theory followed by decisive experiment, though this is a less measurement-oriented topic from my own perspective.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele made the key theoretical proposals. Molenkamp's group gave the HgTe experimental confirmation of the quantum spin Hall state (with the Zhang group's prediction for HgTe, and Zhang is not credited). Hasan's ARPES observation of 3D topological insulators is a third strand. I prefer Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, though that leaves out Hasan.
assessment.maturity: Well confirmed through many independent experiments, including transport and ARPES, and it is clearly an established field. Applications such as dissipationless edge transport are still limited.
uncertainties: Credit is contested among the Kane-Mele, Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang, Molenkamp and Hasan contributions.
A fair prize needs either four people or a choice that leaves out an important contribution.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical coherence tomography gives micrometre-resolution depth imaging of tissue and is standard in ophthalmology, with a large clinical impact. It is the sort of measurement technique that moved from the lab into medicine, and it relates closely to my own work on optical imaging in tissue.
assessment.attribution: The 1991 Science paper by Huang, Swanson and Fujimoto, with Fujimoto's group, is the central demonstration. Other groups (Fercher, Hitzenberger, Izatt and others) have contributed to the field, notably Fourier-domain OCT, and are not listed. The credited names are consistent with the original invention.
assessment.maturity: Mature, with strong independent adoption and decades of clinical use. Recognition would be timely, though there may be a question of whether it sits in physics or in medicine or engineering.
uncertainties: Whether the committee sees this as a physics discovery or invention within the will of Nobel is uncertain.
Credit may be disputed with Fercher and Fourier-domain contributors, which I have not verified in detail.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED made strong coupling of superconducting artificial atoms to microwave photons routine, and it underlies superconducting quantum processors, dispersive readout and cavity-based quantum measurement. The experimental accumulation of coherence and control is exemplary.
assessment.attribution: Blais and colleagues proposed the architecture, Wallraff and Schoelkopf (with Yale and ETH) demonstrated strong coupling in 2004. Those three form a natural combination. Devoret and others are outside this list.
assessment.maturity: Highly mature and widely reproduced. As I understand it, a recent prize recognised related superconducting circuit work, which may reduce urgency for this topic, though I have not verified the details.
uncertainties: Overlap with recent recognition of macroscopic quantum effects in superconducting circuits may make a repeat in the same area less likely.
Credit among Devoret, Schoelkopf, Wallraff and Blais is intertwined.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The qPlus sensor with CO-functionalised tips gave atomic-resolution AFM of single molecules, imaging of bond structure and charge states. This is a real step in measurement capability, with strong experimental demonstration at the single-molecule level.
assessment.attribution: Giessibl invented the qPlus sensor. Gross and Meyer at IBM Zurich demonstrated the functionalised tips and the molecular bond imaging in 2009. The three form a plausible trio, but the field includes other contributors to frequency-modulation AFM (Albrecht, Quate and Binnig for AFM itself).
assessment.maturity: Techniques are replicated across many labs, but the scope is more specialised than the larger candidates above. It is mature but may be premature as a prize compared with broader fields.
uncertainties: The relevance to the broad community is narrower than for other candidates.
Overlap with earlier STM and AFM recognition (1986 prize) could limit novelty in the committee's view.
